The IANA functions coordinate the Internet’s globally unique identifiers, and are provided by Public Technical Identifiers , an affiliate of ICANN .

For the Internet to work as a single seamless network, technical identifiers must mean the same thing everywhere: network identifiers like domain names and IP addresses must be assigned to a single party and have the same meaning globally, and communication protocols must use codes that have the same interpretation by every software implementation. The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) maintains the authoritative public registries that record these allocations and definitions, providing a common global point of reference.

Although the Internet is decentralized by design, a limited set of its technical elements require this globally coordinated administration. The IANA role is a public service. The registries we maintain are openly published, our services are provided without charge, and we act as a neutral steward implementing policies developed by the communities we serve. Much of our work involves processing requests for identifiers arising from technical standardization processes or submitted directly by users of IANA services. We assess each request carefully against the established policies governing the identifier’s allocation and use.

Our responsibilities extend beyond maintaining the registries themselves. We also operate the systems used to publish the registries and their associated data, together with supporting operational services. These include infrastructure and events involved in producing, securing, and distributing key aspects of the DNS.
The need for the IANA functions dates to the record-keeping activities that accompanied the earliest experiments leading to today’s Internet, and their origins can be traced to the 1970s. Today, the functions are performed by Public Technical Identifiers , a purpose-built affiliate of ICANN dedicated exclusively to delivering the IANA services.

Domain Name Services
We operate and maintain a number of key aspects of the DNS, including the root zone, and the .int and .arpa domains.
The DNS Root Zone The root is the upper-most part of the DNS hierarchy, and involves delegating administrative responsibility of “top-level domains”, which are the last segment of a domain name.
.INT The .int top-level domain, designed for the sole use of cross-national organisations, such as treaty organisations, that do not naturally fit into a specific country’s top-level domain.
.ARPA The .arpa domain is used internally by Internet protocols for purposes not designed to be directly accessed, as defined in various technical standards.
IDN Practices Repository A repository of permissible characters for different languages and writing systems provided for registration by different domain registries, helping to foster internationalization.

Root Key Signing Key (DNSSEC) The Root Key Signing Key provides verification of the DNSSEC-signed root zone, administered through public key signing ceremonies and serving as the DNS trust anchor.
Reserved Domains Specially designated domains that are held to serve specialized purposes, such as avoiding conflicts with potential real-world usage.
